summary:
Same-sex activity has been legal in Panama since a 2008 presidential decree resting on constitutional nondiscrimination grounds. No traveller-facing restrictions are in force: there are no bathroom or facilities laws, no documented inspection of gender markers at Panamanian border crossings, and no recorded pattern of police targeting trans visitors.

Legal gender recognition exists but requires surgery, and no nonbinary recognition is available. A visitor whose passport carries a marker inconsistent with presentation has no documented record of friction at entry points, though the surgery requirement determines which documents residents can obtain in the first place.

No statute prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The National Assembly blocked an amendment to the general anti-discrimination law in 2024, and a 2015 bill covering both grounds has not advanced. Equaldex records no employment or housing discrimination protections, and no acts are formally recognised as hate crimes.

Partner recognition is restricted. Article 40 of the Code of Private International Law, approved 8 May 2014, states that same-sex marriages are strictly prohibited and that foreign same-sex marriages will not be recognised. On 27 March 2023, after a seven-year delay, the Supreme Court ruled that there is no positive right to same-sex marriage under the constitution. A constitutional amendment defining marriage as between a man and a woman was approved by the National Assembly on 29 October 2019 but withdrawn before referendum following public protests.

Marriage litigation ran through 2017 and 2018. Justice Luis Ramón Fábrega's October 2017 draft ruling held the family code's same-sex marriage bars not unconstitutional while leaving the National Assembly to legislate civil unions; he withdrew that draft in February 2018, and the government signalled it would comply with the 9 January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights decision. Two lawsuits, a UK-marriage recognition suit and a direct family-code challenge, were combined after summer 2017 oral arguments.

Health and bodily-autonomy rules carry direct consequences. Gay and bisexual men are barred from donating blood under an indefinite deferral. Conversion therapy is not banned. Intersex infant surgeries are not prohibited or regulated.

Reform efforts remain stalled. At the 2025 UN Universal Periodic Review multiple states urged Panama to adopt explicit anti-discrimination protections, reform gender recognition and strengthen safeguards against violence. The country lags much of the region on these measures, and public opinion is unsupportive: 12% approve of same-sex marriage (AmericasBarometer 2023, ranked 18th of 22 in the Americas), and a 2017 survey found 78% opposed.
tangentialFactors:
Religious and political hostility is documented and shapes the environment around any equality claim. The Roman Catholic Church defeated a 2004 civil-union proposal and condemned the 2018 Inter-American Court advisory opinion, and one deputy labelled that opinion "a danger to the human race"; Catholic and evangelical groups spearheaded opposition to the 2017 marriage suits, while the First Lady publicly supported them.

Article 39 of the Constitution, which bars associations contrary to moral or legal order, has been used to refuse registration to gay organisations. The first gay group, AHMNP, founded 1996, obtained legal recognition only in 2005 after a three-year battle.

Gender diversity is received differently in parts of the country. In the Guna Yala indigenous territory, a flourishing third-gender community (Omeggid) is treated as entirely normal, with matriarchal figures elevating women's status — cultural context that does not extend to national legal protections.

Compared with neighbouring jurisdictions, Panama's package of legal recognition, nondiscrimination coverage and hate-crime machinery is thin, and the 2025 UPR exchange placed that gap on the record internationally.
localsOnly:
Residents seeking legal gender recognition must undergo surgery; there is no route to a marker change otherwise, and no nonbinary option exists on any document.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination in employment, housing or services on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no conduct is classified as a hate crime, so bias-motivated violence is prosecuted, if at all, under ordinary offences.

Residents' own marriages are constrained by Article 40 of the Code of Private International Law, and the 2023 Supreme Court ruling forecloses a constitutional right to same-sex marriage; the withdrawn 2019 amendment left the statutory position as it stands.

Gay and bisexual men face an indefinite deferral from blood donation. Conversion therapy remains unregulated, and intersex infants may undergo surgery without legal prohibition.

Organising carries registration risk under Article 39 of the Constitution, which has been applied against LGBT groups historically.

In Guna Yala, the Omeggid third gender is accepted within community life, a local cultural standing that carries no legal status nationally.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents how Panamanian border or immigration officers treat a passport gender marker that conflicts with presentation. The absence of recorded friction is not the same as a stated policy, and no entry-screening procedure for trans travellers is sourced.

Whether Article 40's refusal to recognise foreign same-sex marriages has been applied to visitors presenting foreign marriage documents at the border, in hospitals or in consular settings is unresolved; the provision's text is sourced, its visitor-facing enforcement is not.

The inventory gives no enforcement data on violence against trans people in Panama, no figures on incidents, prosecutions or police response, and no trans-specific homicide or assault counts.

Whether Panama accepted, rejected or noted the 2025 UPR recommendations on SOGI protections, gender recognition and violence safeguards is not sourced here.

Prevalence of conversion practice and the clinical extent of intersex infant surgery are not quantified in the inventory; only their unregulated legal status is documented.

The 2017 and 2023 survey figures measure attitudes toward same-sex marriage, not toward trans people specifically; no trans-specific public opinion data is available.
